questions.explanation: Once the situation is understood through context analysis, the planner sets the communication objectives the plan must achieve. Option A is the last stage, and options D and C come only after strategy and the communications mix are decided.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: Which sequence best reflects the main stages of the Marketing Communications Planning Framework?

options.a: Resources, strategy, mix, objectives, context analysis, control, schedule
options.b: Objectives, control, context analysis, resources, strategy, schedule, mix
options.c: Context analysis, objectives, strategy, coordinated mix, schedule, resources, control and evaluation
options.d: Mix, schedule, objectives, context analysis, resources, strategy, control

questions.explanation: The MCPF moves from understanding the situation (context analysis) to deciding goals (objectives), then the overall approach (strategy), the tools and media (coordinated mix), timing (schedule), budget and people (resources), and finally control and evaluation. Options B, D and A scramble this logic, for example setting goals before the situation is understood.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT usually examined in the context analysis stage of the MCPF?

options.a: The final evaluation of the campaign's results
options.b: The customer context, such as buyers' needs and behaviour
options.c: The internal context, such as the firm's resources and culture
options.d: The business context, such as competitors and the market

questions.explanation: Context analysis looks at the customer, business, internal and external (wider environment) contexts before planning begins. Measuring the campaign's results, option A, belongs to the control and evaluation stage at the end.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: Before planning a campaign, a Nigerian telecom firm studies new government regulations, inflation and changes in technology. These belong to which part of the MCPF context analysis?

options.a: The coordinated communications mix
options.b: The control and evaluation stage
options.c: The internal context
options.d: The external (wider environment) context

questions.explanation: Regulation, the economy and technology are wider environmental (PEST-type) factors, so they form the external context. Option C concerns the firm's own resources and culture, option B is the end-of-plan review, and option A is the choice of tools and media.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: Marketing communication objectives in the MCPF are usually derived from:

options.a: The personal preferences of the advertising agency
options.b: The colour scheme of the company logo
options.c: The corporate and marketing objectives of the organisation
options.d: Whatever competitors spent last year

questions.explanation: Communication objectives follow from the firm's corporate and marketing objectives, so MarCom supports the wider business goals. Options A, D and B are not a proper basis for objectives.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: When setting marketing communication objectives, the SMART principle requires objectives to be:

options.a: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time-bound
options.b: Sales-based, Market-wide, Aggressive, Rapid and Targeted
options.c: Simple, Mass, Attractive, Repeated and Televised
options.d: Strategic, Monetary, Annual, Regional and Tactical

questions.explanation: SMART objectives are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time-bound, which makes it possible to judge whether the plan worked. The expansions in options C, D and B are invented.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: A Lagos juice company states: "Increase awareness of our new brand among undergraduates in Lagos from 20% to 45% within six months." Why is this a well-written MarCom objective?

options.a: It avoids any measurable figure
options.b: It is specific, measurable and time-bound, with a clear target audience and benchmark
options.c: It sets no time limit, so it cannot fail
options.d: It mentions juice, which every objective must do

questions.explanation: The objective names the audience (Lagos undergraduates), a starting point and target (20% to 45%) and a deadline (six months), which makes it SMART and in line with DAGMAR. Option D is irrelevant, and options A and C describe the very things the objective avoids.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: In MarCom strategy, a pull strategy is directed mainly at:

options.a: End-user consumers, to encourage them to ask for and buy the product
options.b: The firm's own production staff
options.c: Wholesalers and retailers, to encourage them to stock the product
options.d: All stakeholders, to build corporate reputation

questions.explanation: A pull strategy targets end users so that their demand pulls the product through the distribution channel. Option C describes a push strategy aimed at intermediaries, option D is a profile strategy, and option B is internal.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: A detergent maker gives extra margins and display allowances to distributors and supermarkets in Kano so they will stock and promote its brand. This is an example of a:

options.a: Profile strategy
options.b: Push strategy
options.c: Two-step flow
options.d: Pull strategy

questions.explanation: A push strategy directs communication and incentives at channel intermediaries so that they push the product on towards consumers. Option D targets end users directly, option A builds the corporate image among all stakeholders, and option C is a communication model.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: A profile strategy in marketing communications is aimed at:

options.a: Only first-time buyers of a product
options.b: Only retailers who stock the product
options.c: A wide range of stakeholders, to build the organisation's corporate image and reputation
options.d: Only the firm's competitors

questions.explanation: A profile strategy communicates with stakeholders such as investors, employees, government and the community to build the organisation's identity and reputation, rather than to sell a particular product. Options B, A and D are too narrow or wrong.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: The 'coordinated communications mix' stage of the MCPF involves:

options.a: Choosing and combining the tools, media and messages so they work together
options.b: Studying the external environment
options.c: Deciding the firm's corporate mission
options.d: Measuring the campaign's final results

questions.explanation: At this stage the planner selects and integrates the right tools (such as advertising, sales promotion and PR), the media and the content, so they deliver a consistent message. Option B is context analysis, option D is control and evaluation, and option C is corporate strategy.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: In the MCPF, the scheduling (implementation) stage is concerned with:

options.a: When each communication activity will happen and in what order
options.b: How the competitors set their prices
options.c: Which consumers liked the last campaign
options.d: Why the firm exists

questions.explanation: Scheduling sets out the timing and order of activities so that, for example, PR and adverts build awareness before sales promotions push purchase. Options D, B and C belong to corporate mission, competitor analysis and evaluation.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: The 'resources' stage of the MCPF mainly deals with:

options.a: The market share of competitors
options.b: The budget, people and time needed to carry out the plan
options.c: The design of the company logo
options.d: The firm's raw materials for production

questions.explanation: Resources covers the money (the communication budget), staff and agency support, and time needed to put the plan into action. Options D, A and C are production, competitor and design matters.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: Six weeks after a campaign launch, a Port Harcourt restaurant checks whether awareness rose to the target and adjusts its adverts where it fell short. Which MCPF stage is this?

options.a: Control and evaluation
options.b: Scheduling
options.c: Setting objectives
options.d: Context analysis

questions.explanation: Control and evaluation compares actual results with the objectives and makes corrections, and the feedback goes into future planning. Option D happens before planning, option C sets the targets in the first place, and option B is about timing.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: What is the role of feedback in the Marketing Communications Planning Framework?

options.a: It ends the plan so that no further changes are made
options.b: It is used only to calculate the budget
options.c: Results from evaluation feed back into earlier stages so that future plans improve
options.d: It replaces the context analysis

questions.explanation: Feedback loops the lessons from evaluation back into context analysis and objective-setting, so planning is a continuous cycle rather than a one-off. Option A is the opposite of this, option B is too narrow, and option D is wrong because feedback adds to the analysis rather than replacing it.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: Context analysis is considered the foundation of a MarCom plan because:

options.a: It decides the price of the product
options.b: It provides the information on which objectives, strategy and the mix are based
options.c: It is the only stage that costs money
options.d: It is carried out after the campaign is finished

questions.explanation: Every later decision, such as which objectives to set, which strategy to use and which tools to choose, depends on understanding the situation, which is what context analysis supplies. Option C is false, option D describes evaluation, and option A is a pricing decision.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: SOSTAC, a widely used marketing planning model, stands for:

options.a: Situation, Objectives, Strategy, Tactics, Action, Control
options.b: Sales, Orders, Stock, Turnover, Accounts, Costs
options.c: Source, Objective, Signal, Target, Audience, Channel
options.d: Segment, Offer, Sell, Track, Adjust, Close

questions.explanation: SOSTAC moves from situation analysis to objectives, strategy, tactics, action and control, the same logic used in MarCom planning. Options B, C and D are invented expansions.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: A planner states the overall approach for a new campaign: "Position our bank as the friendliest choice for students, using a pull strategy built mainly on social media." This statement belongs to which MCPF stage?

options.a: Marketing communications strategy
options.b: Context analysis
options.c: Resources
options.d: Control and evaluation

questions.explanation: Strategy sets the overall direction of the plan, such as positioning and whether to use pull, push or profile approaches. Option B is research into the situation, option D is checking results, and option C is the budget and staff needed.

questions.topic: Models of Marketing Communication and MarCom Planning
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a stage of the Marketing Communications Planning Framework?

options.a: Control and evaluation
options.b: Recruitment of factory workers
options.c: Context analysis
options.d: Communication objectives

questions.explanation: The MCPF stages are context analysis, objectives, strategy, the coordinated communications mix, scheduling, resources, and control and evaluation. Recruiting factory workers, option B, is a human resources task outside MarCom planning.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: The marketing communications mix is best described as encompassing:

options.a: A blend of advertising, sales promotion, public relations and personal selling
options.b: Product, price, place and promotion
options.c: Segmentation, targeting and positioning
options.d: Source, message, medium and receiver

questions.explanation: The marketing communications mix is the set of promotional tools, traditionally advertising, sales promotion, personal selling, public relations and direct marketing, used in combination to reach a target audience. Option B is the wider marketing mix, of which promotion is only one part. Option C is about choosing markets and D lists the parts of the communication process.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: The marketing communication context refers to:

options.a: Only the words and pictures used in an advertisement
options.b: Only the size of the firm's advertising budget
options.c: The circumstances, inside and outside the organisation, in which communication takes place and is interpreted
options.d: Only the price at which the product is sold

questions.explanation: Context covers the setting that shapes how messages are planned and understood, such as customers, competitors, the wider environment and the organisation itself. Options A, B and D each pick out a single item, the message, the budget or the price, and treat it as if it were the whole context.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Factors that influence the choice of marketing communication mix are grouped into product, customer, organisation, and competition and situation related factors. Under which group does the communication budget fall?

options.a: Product related factors
options.b: Organisation related factors
options.c: Customer related factors
options.d: Competition and situation related factors

questions.explanation: The budget is a resource controlled by the firm itself, so it sits with the marketing channel adopted and branding strategy under organisation related factors. Option A covers things like product complexity, life cycle stage and unit price, C covers target market characteristics and the type of buying decision, and D covers the firm's visibility, environment and competition.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: When choosing the marketing communication mix, the stage of the product in its life cycle is classified as a:

options.a: Customer related factor
options.b: Organisation related factor
options.c: Product related factor
options.d: Competition and situation related factor

questions.explanation: Product related factors include the amount and complexity of product information, the product's life cycle stage, and the product type and unit price. Option A deals with the target market and type of buying decision, B with channels, branding and budget, and D with the firm's visibility, environment and competitors.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Within the marketing communications mix, advertising primarily serves to:

options.a: Offer short-term incentives such as coupons to trigger immediate sales
options.b: Win unpaid coverage in the editorial section of the news media
options.c: Build brand recognition and reinforce market presence through paid media
options.d: Build personal relationships through face-to-face selling

questions.explanation: Advertising is a paid, indirect way of reaching many people through TV, radio, print and websites, which makes it well suited to building recognition and keeping a brand visible. Option A describes sales promotion, B describes publicity, and D describes personal selling.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Which marketing communication tool is an indirect, paid method of informing customers about goods and services through television, radio, print and websites?

options.a: Publicity
options.b: Personal selling
options.c: Word-of-mouth marketing
options.d: Advertising

questions.explanation: Advertising is paid for by the firm and delivered through mass media rather than in person, which is why it is called indirect. Option A is free coverage in the news media, B is direct contact between a salesperson and a customer, and C happens when customers share their own experiences with friends and peers.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: The role of sales promotion in the marketing communications mix is to:

options.a: Win free editorial coverage in the news media
options.b: Trigger immediate purchase through incentives and short-term offers
options.c: Build the firm's long-term reputation with all stakeholders
options.d: Communicate with each customer face-to-face

questions.explanation: Sales promotion uses incentives such as discounts, coupons, rebates and buy-one-get-one-free offers to give people a reason to buy now. Option A describes publicity, C describes public relations, and D describes personal selling.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Coupons, rebates and buy-one-get-one-free offers are examples of:

options.a: Publicity
options.b: Sales promotion
options.c: Public relations
options.d: Direct marketing

questions.explanation: Each of these gives the buyer an extra incentive to purchase in the short term, which is what sales promotion is about. Option A is unpaid news coverage, C is about managing the firm's reputation, and D is personalised communication such as emails, brochures and telemarketing sent directly to individuals.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Public relations within the marketing communications mix is mainly used to:

options.a: Offer short-term price discounts to boost sales
options.b: Enhance the firm's reputation and credibility through earned media
options.c: Buy time and space on television and radio
options.d: Persuade individual customers in one-to-one sales meetings

questions.explanation: Public relations focuses on reputation, using unpaid or earned communication such as press releases, campaigns and crisis management to build good relationships with the media and other stakeholders. Option A is sales promotion, C is advertising, and D is personal selling.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Publicity differs from advertising mainly because publicity:

options.a: Is not paid for and appears as news in the editorial section of the media
options.b: Is always delivered face-to-face by a salesperson
options.c: Relies on coupons, rebates and discounts
options.d: Is aimed only at the firm's own employees

questions.explanation: Publicity promotes to the mass market like advertising does, but it is free and depends on the media finding the story newsworthy, for example through press releases, photos and feature stories. Option B describes personal selling, C describes sales promotion, and D is wrong because publicity reaches the general public.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Personal selling in the marketing communications mix is characterised by:

options.a: Mass media campaigns aimed at very large audiences
options.b: Coupons and rebates that encourage quick purchase
options.c: Unpaid coverage of the firm in the news media
options.d: Tailored, face-to-face interaction that addresses each customer's needs

questions.explanation: In personal selling a salesperson approaches prospects directly and uses skills to build personal relationships, adapting the message to each person. Option A describes advertising, B describes sales promotion, and C describes publicity.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: An external factor within the marketing communication context is:

options.a: The company's internal policies and procedures
options.b: Competitive positioning and market trends
options.c: The organisation's culture and values
options.d: The firm's own staff performance appraisals

questions.explanation: Competitors and market trends exist outside the firm, so they belong to the external context that communication plans must respond to. Options A, C and D all come from inside the organisation, so they are internal factors.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Selection criteria for the marketing communications mix are used to:

options.a: Ensure every promotional tool receives an equal share of the budget
options.b: Choose tools based only on what competitors are using
options.c: Remove the need to set communication objectives
options.d: Identify and prioritise the tools that will be most effective for the audience and objectives

questions.explanation: Factors such as the product, the customer, the organisation and the competitive situation help a firm decide which tools to use and how heavily to use each one. Option A ignores these differences, B wrongly treats competition as the only factor, and C is wrong because tools are chosen to meet objectives.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: The marketing communications mix is designed to:

options.a: Set the firm's production targets
options.b: Reach and persuade the intended audience effectively across channels
options.c: Decide where the firm's factories are located
options.d: Determine the wages paid to the sales force

questions.explanation: The mix combines tools such as advertising, sales promotion, public relations, personal selling and direct marketing in different degrees so that the target audience receives and acts on the firm's messages. Options A and C are production decisions and D is a human resources decision.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Which of the following is an element of the marketing communications mix?

options.a: Product design as a competitive differentiator
options.b: Public relations as a tool for reputation management
options.c: Pricing strategy as a way of signalling value
options.d: Inventory management as a way of controlling costs

questions.explanation: Public relations is one of the traditional tools of the marketing communications mix, alongside advertising, sales promotion, personal selling and direct marketing. Options A and C belong to the wider marketing mix (product and price), and D is an operations activity.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the five traditional tools of the marketing communications mix?

options.a: Direct marketing
options.b: Personal selling
options.c: Pricing
options.d: Public relations

questions.explanation: The five traditional tools are advertising, sales promotion, personal selling, public relations and direct marketing. Pricing is part of the wider marketing mix, not the communications mix, while options A, B and D are all communication tools.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: The set of tools that can be used in various combinations and different degrees of intensity in order to communicate with a target audience is called the:

options.a: Marketing communications context
options.b: Media schedule
options.c: Marketing communications mix
options.d: Product life cycle

questions.explanation: The marketing communications mix is the combination of tools such as advertising, sales promotion, personal selling, public relations and direct marketing, used in different mixes and intensities to reach a target audience. Option A refers to the circumstances in which communication takes place, not the tools themselves. Option B is only a timetable for placing adverts.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Traditionally, the five main tools of the marketing communications mix are advertising, sales promotion, personal selling, public relations and:

options.a: Direct marketing
options.b: Packaging
options.c: Pricing
options.d: Distribution

questions.explanation: Direct marketing completes the traditional five tools of the communications mix. Packaging, pricing and distribution in options B, C and D are elements of the wider marketing mix, not tools of the communications mix.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Advertising, as a tool of the marketing communications mix, is best described as:

options.a: An indirect, paid way of informing customers about goods and services through media such as TV, radio, print and websites
options.b: Face-to-face presentation by a salesperson who builds personal relationships with prospects
options.c: Short-term incentives such as coupons and rebates offered to boost sales quickly
options.d: Free coverage of newsworthy events about a firm in the editorial section of the news media

questions.explanation: Advertising is a paid, non-personal (indirect) method of communicating with customers through mass media. Option D describes publicity, which is not paid for, option B describes personal selling, and option C describes sales promotion.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Which of the following are the most common forms of publicity?

options.a: Telemarketing calls and catalogues
options.b: Coupons, rebates and premiums
options.c: News releases, photos and feature stories
options.d: Billboards, radio jingles and TV commercials

questions.explanation: News releases (press releases), photos and feature stories are the usual ways firms get free editorial coverage. Option B lists sales promotion tools, option A lists direct marketing tools and option D lists paid advertising.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: The form of marketing communication that focuses on the firm's reputation through unpaid or earned communication, building positive relationships with media figures and other stakeholders, is:

options.a: Public relations
options.b: Advertising
options.c: Direct marketing
options.d: Sales promotion

questions.explanation: Public relations is concerned with the organisation's reputation and its relationships with the media and other stakeholders, mostly through earned rather than paid communication. Option B is paid communication in bought media space, while options C and D aim at boosting sales through incentives or personalised offers.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Which of the following activities is typically part of public relations?

options.a: Buying a 30-second TV commercial
options.b: Telemarketing to a customer list
options.c: A buy-one-get-one-free offer
options.d: Crisis management

questions.explanation: Crisis management, along with press releases and communication campaigns, is a core PR activity used to protect reputation and relationships with stakeholders. Option C is a sales promotion, option B is direct marketing and option A is paid advertising.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: After a rumour spread online that its bottled water was contaminated, a Lagos water company held a press conference, issued a press release and invited journalists to tour its factory. Which communication tool is the company mainly using?

options.a: Sales promotion
options.b: Personal selling
options.c: Direct marketing
options.d: Public relations

questions.explanation: Responding to a rumour with press conferences, press releases and media tours is public relations, specifically crisis management aimed at protecting the firm's reputation. Option A would involve incentives such as discounts, and option C would involve personalised messages to individual customers.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: The area of marketing communications that aims to stimulate sales through incentives, short-term discounts and other promotional offers is:

options.a: Advertising
options.b: Personal selling
options.c: Sales promotion
options.d: Public relations

questions.explanation: Sales promotion uses short-term incentives and offers to give people an extra reason to buy now. Option D is about reputation, option B is face-to-face selling, and option A is paid mass-media communication that does not by itself offer an incentive.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a sales promotion technique?

options.a: Coupons
options.b: Buy-one-get-one-free offers
options.c: Rebates
options.d: A press release

questions.explanation: A press release is a publicity and PR tool used to gain free news coverage. Coupons, rebates and buy-one-get-one-free offers, options A, B and C, are all incentives used in sales promotion.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: A Surulere supermarket announces that, this weekend only, any customer who buys two packs of noodles gets a third pack free. This is an example of:

options.a: Direct marketing
options.b: Sales promotion
options.c: Publicity
options.d: Public relations

questions.explanation: A time-limited 'buy two, get one free' offer is a short-term incentive to boost sales, which is sales promotion. Option C would be free news coverage, and option D would focus on reputation rather than an immediate offer.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Personal selling is best described as:

options.a: Free coverage of a firm's activities in newspapers and on the television news
options.b: Paid, one-way communication to a mass audience through TV and radio broadcasts
options.c: Face-to-face communication in which a salesperson informs prospects and builds relationships
options.d: An online catalogue that lets customers place orders with no human contact

questions.explanation: Personal selling involves a salesperson approaching prospects directly, mostly face to face, to inform them and build relationships. Option B describes advertising, option A describes publicity, and option D lacks the personal salesperson contact that defines personal selling.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Personal selling is regarded as one of the most reliable modes of marketing communication mainly because:

options.a: It reaches millions of people at the same moment
options.b: It has the lowest cost per customer contacted
options.c: It relies on the news media to carry the message free of charge
options.d: It is done directly with the prospect, orally face to face or in writing

questions.explanation: Personal selling is considered reliable because the seller deals directly with the prospect and can respond to that person. Options A and B describe advertising strengths; personal selling actually reaches few people and costs a lot per contact. Option C describes publicity.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Direct marketing differs from advertising on mass media mainly because direct marketing:

options.a: Communicates directly with individuals in a more personalised way
options.b: Is aimed at the general public rather than at selected individuals
options.c: Appears only in the editorial section of newspapers
options.d: Is always provided free of charge by the media

questions.explanation: Direct marketing is a more personalised form of communication that reaches individuals directly, rather than through general messages on mass media. Option B reverses this, and options C and D describe publicity rather than direct marketing.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of direct marketing?

options.a: Sponsoring a state football tournament
options.b: A personalised email offer sent to customers on a company's mailing list
options.c: A press release sent to newspaper editors
options.d: A television commercial shown during the evening news

questions.explanation: Emails sent to named individuals on a list are a classic direct marketing tool, along with brochures, interactive websites and telemarketing. Option D is mass advertising, option C is publicity, and option A is event sponsorship.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: An Ikeja furniture company mails printed brochures, each addressed by name and with a reply form, to 2,000 customers on its database. Which communication tool is this?

options.a: Event sponsorship
options.b: Direct marketing
options.c: Publicity
options.d: Advertising

questions.explanation: Sending addressed brochures to individuals from a database is direct marketing, because the message goes straight to selected people and invites a response. Option D would use mass media to reach a general audience, and option C would rely on free news coverage.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: When companies sponsor sports, entertainment, non-profit or community events in order to reinforce their brand in customers' minds and create a long-term association, they are using:

options.a: Interactive marketing
options.b: Word-of-mouth marketing
options.c: Events and experiences
options.d: Direct marketing

questions.explanation: Events and experiences (sponsorship) link the brand to activities that customers value, giving brand exposure and a lasting association. Option A is about customers interacting with the firm online, and option B is customers sharing experiences with friends.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: A telecom company pays to have its name attached to a university inter-faculty football competition, with its logo on jerseys and banners throughout the season. This is mainly an example of:

options.a: Sales promotion
options.b: Events and experiences (sponsorship)
options.c: Direct marketing
options.d: Personal selling

questions.explanation: Paying to associate a brand with a sports event for exposure is sponsorship, which falls under events and experiences. Option D needs a salesperson dealing with prospects, and option A needs a short-term incentive to buy, neither of which is present here.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: An online store lets customers ask questions and get them resolved online, and shows each customer what they chose or ordered in the recent past. This approach is called:

options.a: Interactive marketing
options.b: Word-of-mouth marketing
options.c: Publicity
options.d: Personal selling

questions.explanation: Interactive marketing lets customers interact with the firm online and get their queries resolved there, as on Amazon. Option B involves customers talking to their peers, not to the firm, and option D needs a salesperson approaching the prospect.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: The communication tool in which customers share their experiences of goods and services they recently bought with their peers and friends is:

options.a: Word-of-mouth marketing
options.b: Public relations
options.c: Interactive marketing
options.d: Direct marketing

questions.explanation: Word-of-mouth marketing happens when customers pass on their experiences to friends and peers. Option C is interaction between customer and firm, and option D is personalised communication sent by the firm itself.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Apart from the communication tools, the marketing communications mix also includes media, which are best described as:

options.a: The customers who receive and interpret the firm's messages
options.b: The channels in which time and space can be bought or used to deliver messages to target audiences
options.c: The incentives offered to customers to boost short-term sales
options.d: The staff who design and manufacture the product

questions.explanation: Media are the channels, such as TV, radio, newspapers or websites, in which time and space are bought or used to carry messages to the audience. Option A describes receivers, and option C describes sales promotion.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Which communication tool is generally regarded by audiences as the most credible?

options.a: Advertising
options.b: Public relations
options.c: Direct marketing
options.d: Sales promotion

questions.explanation: PR messages usually reach people through third parties such as journalists, so audiences see them as more believable than messages the firm pays for. Option A, advertising, is often viewed with suspicion because everyone knows the firm paid to say good things about itself.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Which communication tool gives the organisation the LEAST control over the final message that reaches the audience?

options.a: Sales promotion
options.b: Advertising
options.c: Public relations (publicity)
options.d: Direct marketing

questions.explanation: With publicity, the media decide whether to use the story and how to present it, so the firm has little control over the final message. With advertising, direct marketing and sales promotion, options A, B and D, the firm pays for or designs the message and decides its content and timing.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Which communication tool usually has the highest cost per contact?

options.a: Sales promotion
options.b: Public relations
options.c: Advertising
options.d: Personal selling

questions.explanation: Personal selling requires a salesperson's time, travel and pay for each prospect, so the cost of each contact is high. Option C, advertising, may cost a lot in total but spreads that cost over a very large audience, giving a low cost per contact.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Which communication tool allows the greatest two-way interaction and immediate feedback from the customer?

options.a: Sales promotion
options.b: Personal selling
options.c: Advertising
options.d: Public relations

questions.explanation: In personal selling the seller and buyer talk directly, so the seller can see reactions, answer questions and adjust the message immediately. Advertising, option C, is largely one-way communication with delayed feedback.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: A major weakness of advertising compared with personal selling is that advertising:

options.a: Cannot reach a large and widely spread audience
options.b: Is largely one-way and impersonal, so it cannot adapt to each person's questions
options.c: Has a very high cost per person reached
options.d: Gives the firm no control over the content of the message

questions.explanation: Advertising talks at the audience rather than with them, so it cannot respond to each individual the way a salesperson can. Options A and C are actually advertising's strengths reversed, since it reaches large audiences at a low cost per contact, and option D is wrong because the advertiser controls the message.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: A major strength of advertising is its ability to:

options.a: Close sales through face-to-face negotiation with each buyer
options.b: Obtain coverage in the news media without paying for it
options.c: Deliver a message tailored to one person at a time
options.d: Reach a large, geographically dispersed audience at a low cost per contact

questions.explanation: Advertising can repeat a message many times to a mass audience spread over a wide area, and the cost per person reached is low. Options A and C are strengths of personal selling, and option B describes publicity.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: A main weakness of relying heavily on sales promotion is that it:

options.a: Mainly gives short-term sales gains and can make buyers wait for deals
options.b: Takes many years before it has any noticeable effect on sales
options.c: Is seen as the most credible tool because journalists deliver it
options.d: Cannot be measured in any way, so its results are unknown

questions.explanation: Sales promotion gives a quick, short-term lift in sales, but frequent deals can make customers wait for offers and weaken the brand's image. Option B is the opposite, since promotions work fast, and option C describes publicity, not sales promotion.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: The main strength of publicity compared with advertising is that:

options.a: It allows face-to-face negotiation with each customer
options.b: The firm can decide exactly when and how the story will appear
options.c: It guarantees an immediate increase in sales
options.d: Audiences tend to see it as more believable because it comes from a third party such as the news media

questions.explanation: A story carried by journalists looks like news rather than a sales pitch, so people tend to believe it more. Option B is a weakness turned around, because the media, not the firm, control publicity, and option A describes personal selling.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: A key weakness of personal selling is that it:

options.a: Reaches relatively few people and is expensive per contact
options.b: Has low credibility because the message is unpaid
options.c: Cannot respond to customers' questions and objections
options.d: Cannot be used for industrial or business products

questions.explanation: Each salesperson can only meet a limited number of prospects, and their pay and expenses make every contact costly. Option C is wrong because answering questions is personal selling's main strength, and option D is wrong because personal selling is especially important for business products.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Which of the following is a common weakness of direct marketing?

options.a: Recipients may see unsolicited mail, calls or emails as intrusive 'junk'
options.b: The message cannot be personalised for individual customers
options.c: Responses to the campaign cannot be measured
options.d: It can only reach the mass market, not selected individuals

questions.explanation: Many people resent unrequested mail, calls or emails, which can irritate them and harm the firm's image. Options B, C and D are wrong because personalisation, measurable responses and reaching selected individuals are exactly what direct marketing does well.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Which set of criteria is commonly used to compare marketing communication tools when selecting the communications mix?

options.a: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
options.b: Product, price, place and promotion
options.c: Awareness, interest, desire and action
options.d: Communication effectiveness, credibility, cost and control

questions.explanation: Tools are compared on how well they communicate with the target audience, how believable they are, what they cost and how much control the firm has over the message. Option B is the marketing mix, option A is SWOT analysis, and option C is the AIDA model of how a message works.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Television advertising is often said to have a high absolute cost but a low cost per contact. This means that:

options.a: The total bill is large, but divided over the very large audience reached, the cost per person is small
options.b: The cost depends only on how many units are eventually sold
options.c: Both the total bill and the cost per person reached are small
options.d: The total bill is small, but the cost per person reached is very large

questions.explanation: Absolute cost is the total amount paid for the campaign, while cost per contact is that amount divided by the number of people reached. Because TV reaches so many people, a large total becomes small per person. Option D reverses the two ideas.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: A new small fashion business in Yaba has very little money for promotion. Which of the following is generally the most cost-effective way for it to gain wide coverage at launch?

options.a: Sending a news release about an interesting launch event to local media
options.b: Sponsoring a national football league for a season
options.c: Hiring a large field sales force to visit customers
options.d: Running a national television advertising campaign

questions.explanation: PR and publicity have a low absolute cost, so a newsworthy launch story can gain coverage without paying for media space. Options B, C and D all require large budgets that a small new business is unlikely to have.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Factors that influence the choice of the marketing communications mix can be grouped into product-related, customer-related, organisation-related and:

options.a: Supplier-related factors
options.b: Media-related factors
options.c: Price-related factors
options.d: Competition and situation related factors

questions.explanation: The four groups of selection factors are product-related, customer-related, organisation-related, and competition and situation related factors. Options A, B and C are not among the four groups; for example, price comes in only as unit price within the product-related group.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Which of the following is a product-related factor in selecting the marketing communications mix?

options.a: The impact of competition
options.b: The promotion budget
options.c: The stage of the product in its life cycle
options.d: The characteristics of the target market

questions.explanation: Product-related factors are the amount and complexity of product information, the stage of the product life cycle, and product type and unit price. Option D is customer-related, option B is organisation-related and option A is a competition and situation factor.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: In selecting the marketing communications mix, the type of buying decision the customer faces is classified as a:

options.a: Customer-related factor
options.b: Product-related factor
options.c: Competition and situation related factor
options.d: Organisation-related factor

questions.explanation: Customer-related factors are the characteristics of the target market and the type of buying decision. Option B covers things like product complexity and life cycle stage, and option D covers channel, branding and budget.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: The marketing channel adopted, the branding strategy and the budget are grouped as which type of factors affecting the choice of communications mix?

options.a: Competition and situation related factors
options.b: Product-related factors
options.c: Organisation-related factors
options.d: Customer-related factors

questions.explanation: These three are decisions and resources inside the firm, so they are organisation-related factors. Option D refers to the target market and buying decision, and option A refers to the firm's visibility, environment and competition.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: The visibility of the firm and its political, legal and social environment, together with the impact of competition, are classified as:

options.a: Competition and situation related factors
options.b: Organisation-related factors
options.c: Product-related factors
options.d: Customer-related factors

questions.explanation: These factors describe the situation the firm finds itself in and the competition it faces, so they form the competition and situation group. Option B covers internal matters such as budget and branding, and option D covers the target market and buying decision.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a product-related factor in choosing the marketing communications mix?

options.a: Product type and unit price
options.b: The amount and complexity of product information to be communicated
options.c: Branding strategies
options.d: The stage of the product in its life cycle

questions.explanation: Branding strategies are an organisation-related factor, alongside the marketing channel and budget. Options A, B and D are the three product-related factors.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: A firm sells expensive, technically complex medical scanners to a small number of hospitals. Which communication tool is it most likely to rely on most heavily?

options.a: Mass television advertising
options.b: Free product samples at supermarkets
options.c: Personal selling
options.d: Coupons and other consumer sales promotions

questions.explanation: When a product is costly, complex and bought by few business buyers, a salesperson is needed to explain details, answer questions and negotiate. Options B and D suit cheap consumer goods, and option A would waste money reaching millions of people who will never buy a scanner.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: For low-priced, frequently bought consumer goods such as soft drinks sold to millions of people, the communications mix usually leans most heavily on:

options.a: Exhibitions at trade fairs only
options.b: Personal selling to each individual buyer
options.c: Negotiations led by senior managers
options.d: Advertising and sales promotion

questions.explanation: Cheap products bought often by a mass market need tools that reach many people at low cost per contact and encourage purchase, which is why advertising and sales promotion dominate. Options B and C are far too costly per buyer for a low-priced item.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: A push promotion strategy involves:

options.a: Communicating with a wide range of stakeholders to build the corporate reputation
options.b: Directing communication such as personal selling and trade promotions at channel members, so they stock and promote the product to end users
options.c: Relying only on customers recommending the product to their friends
options.d: Directing advertising and consumer promotions at final consumers, so they ask retailers for the product

questions.explanation: In a push strategy the producer promotes to wholesalers and retailers, who in turn push the product along the channel to consumers. Option D is a pull strategy, and option A is a profile strategy aimed at corporate reputation.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: A manufacturer spends heavily on TV adverts and consumer coupons so that consumers ask retailers for its brand, which makes retailers order the brand from the manufacturer. This is a:

options.a: Profile strategy
options.b: Push strategy
options.c: Trade promotion strategy
options.d: Pull strategy

questions.explanation: In a pull strategy, communication is aimed at final consumers to create demand that pulls the product through the channel. Option B works the other way, by promoting to intermediaries, and option C is also aimed at intermediaries rather than consumers.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: A new seasoning brand gives wholesalers at Idumota market extra margins, display allowances and regular visits from sales representatives so that they stock it and recommend it to retailers. This is mainly a:

options.a: Profile strategy
options.b: Pull strategy
options.c: Push strategy
options.d: Word-of-mouth strategy

questions.explanation: The effort is directed at wholesalers, the channel intermediaries, using trade incentives and personal selling, which is a push strategy. Option B would target final consumers with advertising and consumer promotions instead.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: A communication strategy aimed at a wide range of stakeholders, such as investors, government and the local community, to build the organisation's corporate reputation rather than to move products through the channel, is called a:

options.a: Profile strategy
options.b: Push strategy
options.c: Pull strategy
options.d: Sales promotion strategy

questions.explanation: A profile strategy focuses on how the organisation as a whole is seen by its stakeholders, building corporate identity and reputation. Options B and C are about moving products to intermediaries and consumers respectively.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: At the introduction stage of the product life cycle, the communications mix typically emphasises:

options.a: Reminder advertising only, since buyers already know the product
options.b: Cutting nearly all promotion to save costs
options.c: Advertising and publicity to build awareness, with sales promotion to encourage trial
options.d: Heavy price-off deals mainly to clear old stock before withdrawal

questions.explanation: A new product is unknown, so advertising and PR are used to build awareness and sales promotion helps persuade people to try it. Option A fits the maturity or decline stages, and options B and D describe the decline stage.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: In the decline stage of the product life cycle, a firm usually:

options.a: Doubles its sales force to explain the product's basic features
options.b: Launches a major PR campaign to introduce the product for the first time
options.c: Reduces promotion to a low level, perhaps keeping some reminder advertising
options.d: Raises advertising sharply to create awareness of a brand-new product

questions.explanation: When sales are falling, most promotion is cut back, with perhaps enough reminder advertising to keep loyal buyers. Options A, B and D describe the heavy awareness-building effort typical of the introduction stage.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: In the maturity stage of the product life cycle, when most buyers already know the brand and competition is intense, which tool tends to become relatively more important?

options.a: Introductory publicity
options.b: Sales promotion
options.c: Personal selling to explain a brand-new concept
options.d: Teaser advertising for a new launch

questions.explanation: In maturity, sales promotion grows in importance relative to advertising, as firms use incentives to defend market share against strong competitors. Options A, C and D are suited to launching something new, when buyers need to learn about it.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: When analysing the context in which marketing communications will take place, the four contexts usually considered are the:

options.a: Introduction, growth, maturity and decline contexts
options.b: Source, message, medium and receiver contexts
options.c: Customer, business, internal and external contexts
options.d: Product, price, place and promotion contexts

questions.explanation: Context analysis looks at the customer context, the business context, the internal context of the organisation and the wider external context. Option D is the marketing mix, option B lists elements of the communication process, and option A lists stages of the product life cycle.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Before planning a campaign, a Kano food company finds that it has a small promotion budget, few staff skilled in social media and a cautious company culture. These findings relate to the:

options.a: Customer context
options.b: Internal context
options.c: External context
options.d: Business context

questions.explanation: The internal context covers what is inside the organisation: its financial resources, staff skills, culture and identity. Option C covers forces outside the firm such as PEST factors, and option A covers the target audience's needs and behaviour.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Political, economic, social and technological (PEST) factors and the organisation's wider stakeholders are analysed as part of the:

options.a: Customer context
options.b: External context
options.c: Internal context
options.d: Business context

questions.explanation: The external context covers forces outside the organisation that it cannot control, such as PEST factors and stakeholders. Option C is about the firm's own resources and culture, and option A is about the target segment.

questions.topic: MarCom Context, Mix and Selection Criteria
questions.question: Analysing the needs, perceptions and decision-making process of the target segment is part of the:

options.a: Internal context
options.b: Customer context
options.c: External context
options.d: Business context

questions.explanation: The customer context is about understanding the target audience: who they are, what they need, how they see the brand and how they make buying decisions. Option A looks inside the firm, and option C looks at wider environmental forces.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: In marketing communication, the source is best identified as:

options.a: The originator of the message, such as a brand or spokesperson
options.b: The channel through which the message is spread
options.c: The audience that interprets the message
options.d: The feedback that shows how effective the message was

questions.explanation: This is where the message starts, for example the company, the brand or a person who speaks for it, and how credible it is affects how the message is received. Option B is the medium, C is the receiver and D is feedback.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: The message in marketing communication refers to:

options.a: The crafted content intended to inform, persuade or evoke a response
options.b: The platform that carries the communication
options.c: The target audience receiving the communication
options.d: The audience's response after receiving the communication

questions.explanation: The message is what is actually said or shown, the words, images and ideas the sender puts together for the audience. Option B is the medium, C is the receiver and D is feedback.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: The receiver in marketing communication is defined as:

options.a: The person or organisation that creates and sends the message
options.b: The intended audience that decodes and responds to the message
options.c: The medium that transmits the message
options.d: The content of the message itself

questions.explanation: The receiver is the person or group the message is aimed at, who interprets (decodes) it and may respond. Option A is the sender, C is the medium, and D is the message.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: The medium in marketing communication is most accurately described as:

options.a: The channel, such as digital platforms or broadcast media, that delivers the message
options.b: The sender who creates the communication
options.c: The audience that receives the message
options.d: The process of assessing the message's impact

questions.explanation: The medium is the route a message travels along, for example television, radio, print, websites or social media. Option B is the sender, C is the receiver and D is evaluation through feedback.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: An opinion leader in marketing communication is best described as:

options.a: A person with little knowledge of or interest in the product category
options.b: A trusted person whose views and recommendations shape other people's attitudes and actions
options.c: A mass medium used to broadcast the firm's messages
options.d: A firm's most junior salesperson

questions.explanation: Opinion leaders are people others look to for advice, so when they speak about a product their peers tend to listen and follow. Option A is the opposite, because opinion leaders usually know a lot about the category, C confuses a person with a medium, and D has nothing to do with social influence.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: For a marketing communication to be effective, its source should be:

options.a: Unknown to the audience so that the message seems neutral
options.b: Paid the highest possible fee, whatever the audience thinks of them
options.c: Perceived as credible, knowledgeable and relevant by the audience
options.d: Unconnected to the product to avoid any appearance of bias

questions.explanation: Audiences are more likely to believe and act on a message when they trust the person or organisation delivering it and see them as linked to the product. Option A removes the trust that comes from a known sender, B focuses on cost rather than credibility, and D weakens the relevance that makes a sender persuasive.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: An effective message in marketing communication should be:

options.a: Ambiguous and open to many interpretations
options.b: Clear, compelling and tailored to the audience's needs and values
options.c: Packed with every product feature, whatever the audience needs
options.d: Exactly the same for every audience segment

questions.explanation: A message works best when the audience can understand it easily and sees something in it that matters to them. Option A invites misunderstanding, C overloads people with information they may not care about, and D ignores the differences between segments.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: A receiver's reaction to a marketing communication depends on:

options.a: Only the size of the firm's advertising budget
options.b: Only the number of times the message is repeated
options.c: The firm's production timelines
options.d: Their own interpretation, cultural background and how relevant the message is to them

questions.explanation: People decode messages through their own experience, culture and needs, so the same advert can mean different things to different receivers. Options A and B are wrong because they claim a single sender-side factor decides everything, and C has no direct effect on how a message is interpreted.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: The medium used in marketing communication should be:

options.a: Selected to match the target audience's media preferences and habits
options.b: Always the cheapest one available
options.c: Always television, because it reaches the most people
options.d: Chosen before the target audience has been identified

questions.explanation: A message only works if it reaches the right people, so the medium should be one the target audience actually uses. Option B puts cost ahead of reach, C ignores audiences who rarely watch television, and D reverses the logical order of planning.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Opinion leaders are important in marketing communication because they:

options.a: Remove the need for any paid advertising
options.b: Increase a message's reach and credibility through their social influence
options.c: Control the firm's distribution channels
options.d: Set the selling price of the product

questions.explanation: When trusted people pass on or endorse a message, it spreads to their followers and peers and is believed more readily. Option A overstates their effect, since firms still use advertising, while C and D are distribution and pricing decisions made by the firm.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: The interplay of source, message, receiver and medium constitutes:

options.a: The marketing mix of product, price, place and promotion
options.b: The stages of the product life cycle
options.c: The framework of the marketing communication process
options.d: The segmentation, targeting and positioning process

questions.explanation: These four elements are the building blocks of any communication, so together they describe how marketing communication works. Option A is the marketing mix, B describes how sales change over a product's life, and D is how firms choose markets.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: A strategically crafted message in marketing communication should:

options.a: Focus only on what the firm wants to say about itself
options.b: Be as long as possible so that nothing is left out
options.c: Use technical terms the audience may not understand
options.d: Connect with the audience's aspirations, problems and motivations

questions.explanation: A message works when the audience recognises its own needs and goals in it, which makes them pay attention and respond. Option A ignores the receiver, B risks losing attention, and C creates a barrier to decoding the message.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Unplanned distortion or interference during the communication process, which can cause the receiver to get a different message from the one the sender sent, is called:

options.a: Noise
options.b: Encoding
options.c: Feedback
options.d: Response

questions.explanation: Noise is anything that disturbs the message on its way, whether physical sounds, clutter from other adverts, or misunderstanding. Option C is the receiver's reply to the sender, and option D is the receiver's reaction after receiving the message.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: A radio jingle for a paint brand is broadcast while loud generator sounds drown it out in many homes, so listeners miss the brand name. In communication terms, the generator sound is:

options.a: Feedback
options.b: Noise
options.c: Decoding
options.d: Encoding

questions.explanation: Noise is interference that prevents the message from being received as intended, and here the generator sound physically blocks the jingle. Option A would be listeners' reactions sent back to the firm, and option D is the firm's job of creating the jingle.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: The part of the receiver's response that is communicated back to the sender is called:

options.a: Noise
options.b: Encoding
options.c: The medium
options.d: Feedback

questions.explanation: Feedback closes the communication loop by telling the sender how the message was received. Option A is interference with the message, and option C is the channel that carries the message.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: After a new advert runs, a company tracks calls to its hotline, changes in sales and comments on its social media page to judge how the message was received. These are all forms of:

options.a: Feedback
options.b: Message sidedness
options.c: Encoding
options.d: Noise

questions.explanation: Calls, sales changes and online comments all carry the audience's response back to the sender, which is feedback. Option D would be interference that distorts the message, and option C is the sender's work of creating the advert.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Communication is most effective when the sender's and receiver's ______ overlap, that is, when they share similar experiences, attitudes and language.

options.a: Fields of experience
options.b: Noise levels
options.c: Media budgets
options.d: Adopter categories

questions.explanation: A field of experience is the background of knowledge, values and language a person brings to communication, and the more sender and receiver share, the better the message is understood. Options B, C and D have nothing to do with shared understanding between the two parties.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: An agency writes an advert full of slang popular with Lagos teenagers, but the product is aimed at elderly rural farmers, who cannot understand the advert. The main communication problem is:

options.a: Too much feedback from the target audience
options.b: Too little overlap between the fields of experience of sender and receiver
options.c: A source with too much expertise
options.d: A message that is two-sided instead of one-sided

questions.explanation: The sender encoded the message in language that the receivers do not share, so they cannot decode it correctly. Option D concerns presenting pros and cons, which is not the issue here, and option A makes no sense because the farmers did not respond at all.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Which of the following is a personal communication channel?

options.a: A television commercial
options.b: A newspaper advertisement
options.c: A salesperson's face-to-face conversation with a customer
options.d: A roadside billboard

questions.explanation: Personal channels involve two or more people communicating directly with each other, such as face to face, by phone or by email, with personal feedback. Options A, B and D are non-personal mass media that carry messages without personal contact or feedback.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Non-personal communication channels include:

options.a: Independent experts speaking with clients
options.b: Salespeople, friends and family members
options.c: Print and broadcast media, display media, atmospheres and events
options.d: Neighbours discussing products over the fence

questions.explanation: Non-personal channels carry messages without personal contact or feedback, and include major media, designed environments (atmospheres) and staged events. Options A, B and D all involve people communicating directly, which makes them personal channels.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: When a buyer's friends, neighbours and family members talk to them about a product, this is which kind of personal communication channel?

options.a: An advocate channel
options.b: A social channel
options.c: An expert channel
options.d: A non-personal channel

questions.explanation: Social channels are made up of neighbours, friends, family and associates talking to target buyers. Option A is company salespeople contacting buyers, and option C is independent experts making statements to buyers.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Which medium offers sight, sound and motion and very wide mass reach, but has a high absolute cost?

options.a: Newspapers
options.b: Television
options.c: Billboards
options.d: Radio

questions.explanation: Television combines pictures, sound and movement and reaches huge audiences, but producing and airing commercials is expensive in total. Option D is audio only, option A has no sound or motion, and option C can show only a short, still message.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: The three basic categories of source characteristics that influence how persuasive a source is are:

options.a: Reach, frequency and impact
options.b: Encoding, decoding and feedback
options.c: Credibility, attractiveness and power
options.d: Awareness, trial and adoption

questions.explanation: A source persuades through credibility (expertise and trustworthiness), attractiveness (similarity, familiarity and likability) and power (ability to reward or punish). Option B lists parts of the communication process, option A lists media planning terms, and option D lists steps in adoption.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Source credibility is made up mainly of the source's:

options.a: Similarity and familiarity
options.b: Reach and frequency
options.c: Power and control
options.d: Expertise and trustworthiness

questions.explanation: A credible source is seen as knowing what it is talking about (expertise) and as being honest and unbiased (trustworthiness). Option A lists parts of source attractiveness, and option C relates to source power.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: A toothpaste advert features a qualified dentist in a clinic explaining how the product helps prevent tooth decay. The advert relies mainly on the source's:

options.a: Expertise
options.b: Physical attractiveness
options.c: Similarity to the audience
options.d: Power

questions.explanation: A dentist is seen as having specialised knowledge about teeth, so the advert draws on source expertise, a part of credibility. Option B would be a good-looking model, option D needs the ability to reward or punish, and option C would be an ordinary person like the viewers.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: The honesty, integrity and believability of a source, that is, the audience's belief that the source has no motive to mislead them, is called:

options.a: Trustworthiness
options.b: Expertise
options.c: Power
options.d: Likability

questions.explanation: Trustworthiness is about whether the audience believes the source is being honest and objective. Option B is about knowledge and skill, which a source can have without being trusted, and option D is affection for the source's looks or personality.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: When a receiver accepts a credible source's view because they believe the information is accurate, so that it becomes part of their own beliefs, the process at work is:

options.a: Selective exposure
options.b: Compliance
options.c: Identification
options.d: Internalisation

questions.explanation: Credibility works through internalisation: the receiver adopts the position because it seems correct and keeps it even when the source is not present. Option C is how attractiveness works, through wanting to be like the source, and option B is how power works, through reward or punishment.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Source attractiveness includes the source's:

options.a: Ability to reward or punish the receiver
options.b: Formal position in a professional body
options.c: Expertise and trustworthiness
options.d: Similarity, familiarity and likability

questions.explanation: Attractiveness covers how similar the source is to the receiver, how familiar the receiver is with the source, and how much the receiver likes the source. Option C describes credibility, and option A describes power.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: A detergent advert shows an ordinary mother of three in a busy Lagos home, just like the women the brand targets, explaining why she uses the product. The advert relies mainly on the source's:

options.a: Formal authority
options.b: Power
options.c: Similarity to the audience
options.d: Expertise

questions.explanation: Viewers who see someone like themselves using the product feel 'she is like me', which is similarity, a part of source attractiveness. Option D would need a specialist such as a chemist, and options A and B need the ability to reward, punish or command.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: A source has power when it can administer rewards or punishments to the receiver. The receiver then goes along with the source's request mainly through:

options.a: Decoding
options.b: Compliance
options.c: Identification
options.d: Internalisation

questions.explanation: Power leads to compliance: the receiver accepts the request to gain a reward or avoid a punishment, not necessarily because they agree. Option D is linked to credibility and option C to attractiveness.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Why is source power rarely usable in mass advertising?

options.a: Powerful sources always cost more than any firm can afford
options.b: Consumers always ignore sources that have expertise
options.c: Advertisers usually cannot reward or punish consumers, nor check whether they comply
options.d: Power works only when the message is carried on radio

questions.explanation: Power depends on being able to reward or punish and to watch whether the receiver complies, which a TV or press advert cannot do, so it is more relevant in personal selling. Options A, B and D are not true statements about power or about consumers.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a commonly cited risk of using a celebrity endorser?

options.a: The celebrity is involved in a scandal that harms the brand's image
options.b: The celebrity endorses so many brands that the endorsement loses impact
options.c: The celebrity attracts attention to the advert
options.d: The celebrity overshadows the product, so viewers remember the star but not the brand

questions.explanation: Attracting attention is actually the main benefit of using a celebrity, not a risk. Options A, B and D are the standard risks: overshadowing the product, overexposure, and negative publicity from the celebrity's behaviour.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: A model appears in a perfume advert only to draw attention and enhance the ad's appearance, but does not deliver any message. The model is a(n):

options.a: Opinion former
options.b: Advocate channel
options.c: Indirect source
options.d: Direct source
