questions.explanation: An indirect source draws attention to the advert without actually delivering the message, while a direct source is a spokesperson who delivers the message or demonstrates the product. Option A is someone with formal expertise whose views are sought, which does not fit a silent model.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: The tendency for the persuasive impact of a message from a low-credibility source to increase over time, as people forget the source but remember the message, is called the:

options.a: Recency effect
options.b: Sleeper effect
options.c: Halo effect
options.d: Primacy effect

questions.explanation: With the sleeper effect, people at first discount a message because the source is not credible, but later the message's influence grows as the link to the source fades. Options A and D concern where arguments are placed in a message, not changes over time due to the source.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: A two-sided message, which presents both good and bad points about a product, is usually most effective when the audience:

options.a: Already strongly favours the brand and is unlikely to hear opposing claims
options.b: Needs a simple message with only one clear conclusion
options.c: Is well educated, initially opposed, or likely to hear competitors' counter-arguments
options.d: Has no interest in the product category

questions.explanation: Educated or sceptical audiences, and those who will hear rival claims, find a balanced message more believable. Option A describes the situation where a one-sided message works best, and option B also favours a simple one-sided appeal.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: An advert for a new smartphone presents only its positive features and says nothing about any drawbacks. This is a:

options.a: Comparative advertisement
options.b: Refutational appeal
options.c: Two-sided message
options.d: One-sided message

questions.explanation: A one-sided message mentions only the positive attributes or benefits of the product. Option C would also admit some weaknesses, and option B would raise the other side and then argue against it.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: A message that presents both sides of an issue and then argues against (refutes) the opposing viewpoint is called a:

options.a: Fear appeal
options.b: Comparative advertisement
options.c: One-sided message
options.d: Refutational appeal

questions.explanation: A refutational appeal raises the opposing argument and then knocks it down, which can help 'inoculate' the audience against competitors' claims. Option C ignores the other side entirely, and option B compares the brand with a named competitor.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Placing the strongest arguments at the beginning of a message, on the basis that information presented first is learned best, relies on the:

options.a: Sleeper effect
options.b: Halo effect
options.c: Recency effect
options.d: Primacy effect

questions.explanation: The primacy effect says that what comes first in a message is most effectively learned and remembered. Option C says the opposite, that what comes last is remembered best, and option A concerns the fading influence of a low-credibility source over time.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Leaving the conclusion of a message open for the audience to draw for themselves is usually more effective when the audience is:

options.a: Less educated and not interested in the product
options.b: Highly educated and highly involved with the product
options.c: Likely to see the message only once and in passing
options.d: Facing a complex issue they may not follow without help

questions.explanation: Educated, involved audiences prefer to work out the conclusion themselves and may resent being told what to think. Options A, C and D describe situations where an explicit conclusion works better, because the audience may not reach the intended conclusion alone.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: A message appeal that focuses on the product's features, quality, economy, value or performance is a(n):

options.a: Fear appeal
options.b: Moral appeal
options.c: Emotional appeal
options.d: Rational (informational) appeal

questions.explanation: Rational appeals relate to the audience's self-interest by showing that the product delivers practical benefits such as quality, value or performance. Option C works on feelings such as love, pride or joy, and option B works on the audience's sense of right and wrong.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: A milk advert shows a mother lovingly feeding her smiling baby, aiming to stir feelings of warmth and care rather than giving product facts. This uses a(n):

options.a: Emotional appeal
options.b: Rational appeal
options.c: Comparative appeal
options.d: Moral appeal

questions.explanation: Emotional appeals try to stir positive or negative feelings that motivate purchase, here love and care. Option B would focus on facts such as vitamin content or price, and option C would compare the milk directly with a rival brand.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Appeals directed to the audience's sense of what is right and proper, often used to urge people to support social causes such as a cleaner environment, are called:

options.a: Rational appeals
options.b: Moral appeals
options.c: Humour appeals
options.d: Comparative appeals

questions.explanation: Moral appeals ask people to do the right thing, which is why they are common in campaigns for social causes. Option A focuses on practical product benefits, and option C tries to amuse the audience.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: For a fear appeal, such as a campaign against drink-driving, to work well, it should generally:

options.a: Show the threat and also give a clear, easy action the audience can take to avoid it
options.b: Be aimed only at people who are not at any risk
options.c: Avoid stating what the danger actually is
options.d: Use the most shocking images possible without offering any solution

questions.explanation: Fear appeals tend to persuade when they combine the threat with a recommended action the audience believes it can carry out. Option D can make people block out the message because there is no way to reduce their fear, and option C removes the threat that makes it a fear appeal.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: A key weakness of using humour in advertising is that:

options.a: The joke can distract attention from the brand and may wear out with repetition
options.b: Humour never succeeds in attracting attention
options.c: Humour can be used only on radio
options.d: Humour always reduces how much people like the advert

questions.explanation: Humour is good at catching attention and creating liking, but viewers may remember the joke and forget the brand, and jokes lose their effect when repeated. Options B and D reverse humour's known strengths, and option C is untrue since humour is used in all media.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: An advert that directly or indirectly names a competitor and compares the brand with it on one or more attributes is called:

options.a: Comparative advertising
options.b: A two-sided message
options.c: Reminder advertising
options.d: A refutational appeal

questions.explanation: Comparative advertising compares the advertised brand with a competitor's, either by name or by clear implication. Option D refutes an opposing argument but need not mention a rival brand, and option B admits the brand's own weaknesses rather than comparing it with a competitor.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Consumers notice only some of the many adverts they are exposed to, interpret them in ways that fit what they already believe, and remember only part of them. On the receiver's side, this filtering is called:

options.a: Selective perception
options.b: Encoding
options.c: The sleeper effect
options.d: Message sidedness

questions.explanation: Selective perception (attention, distortion and retention) explains why the receiver may not get the message the sender intended. Option C concerns source credibility over time, option D concerns the message's structure, and option B is done by the sender.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: A person within a reference group who, because of special skills, knowledge, personality or other characteristics, exerts social influence on others is called a(n):

options.a: Advocate channel
options.b: Opinion leader
options.c: Laggard
options.d: Opinion follower

questions.explanation: Opinion leaders are ordinary members of a group whose advice others seek because of their knowledge or personality. Option D is a person who receives that advice, option C is the last adopter category, and option A is company salespeople contacting buyers.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Opinion formers differ from opinion leaders mainly because opinion formers:

options.a: Are ordinary peers with no formal position whose advice is sought informally
options.b: Are always the last group in society to adopt any new product
options.c: Hold a formal or professional position, e.g. journalists or critics, that gives their views authority
options.d: Never use the mass media to obtain information about products

questions.explanation: Opinion formers influence others because of their formal expertise, profession or position, while opinion leaders are informal peers within a social group. Option A describes opinion leaders, not opinion formers, and options B and D describe neither group.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: A professional food critic, whose influence comes from her formal position, writes a weekly column in a national newspaper reviewing new restaurants. In marketing communication terms, she is best described as a(n):

options.a: Laggard
options.b: Opinion former
options.c: Opinion follower
options.d: Indirect source

questions.explanation: Her influence comes from her professional role as a critic, which makes her an opinion former. Option C would be a reader who takes her advice, and option D is a model who draws attention in an advert without delivering a message.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Tunde is not paid by any company, but friends in his estate always ask his advice before buying phones because he reads technology blogs and tries new devices early. Tunde is a(n):

options.a: Advocate channel
options.b: Laggard
options.c: Opinion former
options.d: Opinion leader

questions.explanation: Tunde is an informal member of his social group whose advice is valued because of his interest and knowledge, which is what an opinion leader is. Option C would need a formal professional position such as a journalist, and option A is a company salesperson.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Which of the following is typically TRUE of opinion leaders?

options.a: They are equally influential across all product categories
options.b: They are paid employees of the brands they recommend
options.c: They usually come from a very different social class from their followers
options.d: They tend to be more exposed to media in their area of interest than their followers

questions.explanation: Opinion leaders tend to follow media related to their interest closely, which is why messages often reach the wider public through them. Option C is wrong because opinion leaders are usually similar to their followers, and option A is wrong because opinion leadership tends to be specific to a product area.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: The two-step flow model of communication holds that:

options.a: The mass media directly and equally influence every member of the audience
options.b: A message must pass through two separate media before it reaches anyone
options.c: Information flows from consumers to the company and then to the media
options.d: Information flows from the mass media to opinion leaders, who then pass it on to the wider population

questions.explanation: In the two-step flow, opinion leaders pick up information from the media and then pass it on and interpret it for others through personal influence. Option A is the one-step (direct) view of media influence, which the two-step model rejected.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: The multi-step flow model improves on the two-step flow model by recognising that:

options.a: Followers never discuss products with one another or with leaders
options.b: Opinion leaders never use the mass media to get information
options.c: Media reach both leaders and followers directly, and influence flows in several directions
options.d: Mass media influence every person directly in exactly one step

questions.explanation: The multi-step model accepts that the media reach opinion leaders and followers alike, and that people influence one another in more than one direction. Option B is wrong because opinion leaders are heavy media users, and option D is the one-step view.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Marketers who apply the two-step flow idea in their communication plans often:

options.a: Target opinion leaders, e.g. with free samples, so they spread the word
options.b: Avoid people who often talk about products with others
options.c: Ignore mass media because opinion leaders never use it
options.d: Direct their messages only at laggards in the market

questions.explanation: If messages pass through opinion leaders, it makes sense to reach them first and encourage them to share their views with followers. Option B works against the model, and option C is wrong because opinion leaders actually make heavy use of media in their area.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: The correct order of the adopter categories, from the first to adopt an innovation to the last, is:

options.a: Innovators, early majority, early adopters, laggards, late majority
options.b: Early adopters, innovators, early majority, late majority, laggards
options.c: Innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, laggards
options.d: Early majority, innovators, early adopters, late majority, laggards

questions.explanation: Innovators adopt first, followed by early adopters, the early majority, the late majority and finally laggards. Option B swaps the first two groups, a common slip, because innovators come before early adopters.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Which adopter category is most closely associated with opinion leadership and is respected within its community?

options.a: Innovators
options.b: Early adopters
options.c: Laggards
options.d: Late majority

questions.explanation: Early adopters are guided by respect, are often opinion leaders in their communities, and adopt new ideas early but carefully. Option A, innovators, are venturesome and try new ideas at some risk, but are often seen as too far ahead of others to be role models.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Consumers who are tradition-bound, suspicious of change, and adopt an innovation only when it has become something of a tradition itself are called:

options.a: Innovators
options.b: Late majority
options.c: Laggards
options.d: Early majority

questions.explanation: Laggards are the last group to adopt and resist change. Option B, the late majority, are sceptical and adopt after most people have, but they are not as tradition-bound as laggards.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: Mobile money services spread quickly in Nigeria partly because many users saw them as clearly better than queuing in banking halls to send money. Which characteristic affecting the rate of adoption does this illustrate?

options.a: Compatibility
options.b: Relative advantage
options.c: Observability
options.d: Complexity

questions.explanation: Relative advantage is the degree to which an innovation appears superior to existing products or ways of doing things. Option A is how well it fits people's values and experiences, and option D is how hard it is to understand or use.

questions.topic: Source, Message, Receiver, Medium and Opinion Leaders
questions.question: The adoption process differs from the diffusion of an innovation because adoption refers to:

options.a: The spread of an innovation through a whole market over time
options.b: The flow of information from the mass media to opinion leaders
options.c: The division of buyers into innovators, early adopters and other categories
options.d: The mental process an individual goes through from first hearing about an innovation to finally adopting it

questions.explanation: Adoption is about one person's journey from awareness to regular use, while diffusion describes how the innovation spreads through the whole population over time. Option A describes diffusion, option C describes adopter categories, and option B describes the two-step flow.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Business communication is most completely defined as:

options.a: Communication that takes place only among employees
options.b: Messages sent only to customers outside the firm
options.c: The exchange of information within and outside the organisation to achieve its goals
options.d: Only written communication such as letters and memos

questions.explanation: Business communication covers internal communication among staff and departments as well as external communication with customers, suppliers and other stakeholders, in spoken, written or electronic form. Options A and B each cover only one direction, and D leaves out spoken and electronic communication.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of business communication?

options.a: Building a prototype of a new product
options.b: Carrying out routine maintenance on factory machines
options.c: Physically counting stock in the warehouse
options.d: Analytical reports circulated to stakeholders

questions.explanation: A report sent to stakeholders passes information from one party to another for a business purpose, which is what business communication means. Options A, B and C are product development, maintenance and stock control activities that do not involve sending a message to anyone.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The communication model in a business context typically comprises:

options.a: Product, price, place and promotion
options.b: Attention, interest, desire and action
options.c: Sender, message, channel, receiver and feedback
options.d: Advertising, sales promotion, public relations and personal selling

questions.explanation: The basic communication model follows a message from the sender, through a channel, to the receiver, with feedback showing the sender whether the message was understood. Option A is the marketing mix (the 4 Ps), Option B is the AIDA sequence of how buyers respond to a message, and Option D lists promotion tools, not the parts of the communication model.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: In the communication model, the stage at which the receiver interprets the symbols in a message to work out its meaning is called:

options.a: Decoding
options.b: Encoding
options.c: Noise
options.d: Feedback

questions.explanation: Decoding is the receiver's side of the process: turning the words, sounds or images received back into meaning. Option B, encoding, is done by the sender when putting an idea into a message, Option C, noise, is anything that distorts the message, and Option D, feedback, is the receiver's response sent back to the sender.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The communication process in business involves:

options.a: Transmitting a message one way while deliberately blocking any feedback
options.b: Decoding a message before the sender has decided what to say
options.c: Setting a product's price and then choosing its distribution outlets
options.d: Encoding an idea into a message, transmitting it through a channel and decoding by the receiver

questions.explanation: Communication starts when the sender encodes an idea into a message, sends it through a channel, and the receiver decodes it to get the meaning. Option A is wrong because feedback is a normal part of the process, not something to block, Option B reverses the order, and Option C describes pricing and distribution decisions rather than communication.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: A common form of business communication is:

options.a: Product manufacturing and assembly
options.b: Oral communication, such as discussions during meetings
options.c: Financial auditing and compliance checks
options.d: Stock-taking of raw materials

questions.explanation: Oral (spoken) communication, such as discussions in meetings, phone calls and presentations, is one of the main forms of business communication, alongside written and non-verbal forms. Options A, C and D are business activities, but none of them is a way of passing messages between people.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The communication model is useful to a business because it:

options.a: Explains how organisational messages are sent and received
options.b: Fixes the selling price of each product
options.c: Removes the need to know the target audience
options.d: Guarantees that every message will be understood

questions.explanation: A communication model is a simple picture of how a message moves from sender to receiver, which helps managers see where communication can succeed or break down. Option D is tempting, but no model can guarantee understanding because noise can still distort a message, Option C is wrong because knowing the receiver is central to the model, and Option B is a pricing decision.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: An effective communication process in business ensures that:

options.a: Customer preferences are ignored for the sake of speed
options.b: Messages are sent without considering the receiver
options.c: Only senior managers are allowed to send messages
options.d: Messages are crafted, delivered and interpreted with clarity and purpose

questions.explanation: The aim of a well-managed communication process is that the intended meaning is created by the sender, carried through a suitable channel and understood by the receiver. Option B and Option A would make communication fail because the receiver's needs shape how a message should be designed, and Option C wrongly limits communication to one group.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of business communication?

options.a: Product design and feature improvement
options.b: Financial planning and budget allocation
options.c: Non-verbal cues, such as body language, that influence how stakeholders see a firm
options.d: Recruitment and sourcing of talent

questions.explanation: Non-verbal communication, such as gestures, facial expressions, posture and dress, passes messages without words and shapes how customers, staff and partners see a business. Options A, B and D are product, finance and HR activities, not forms of communication.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Feedback is a critical element of the communication model because it:

options.a: Is the channel through which the message travels
options.b: Shows the sender how the message was received so it can be corrected or refined
options.c: Is the distortion that interferes with a message
options.d: Is the sender's act of putting an idea into words or symbols

questions.explanation: Feedback is the receiver's response sent back to the sender, and it tells the sender whether the message was understood so it can be adjusted. Option A describes the channel or medium, Option C describes noise, and Option D describes encoding.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Strategically, the communication process in business supports:

options.a: Reducing contact with customers to cut costs
options.b: Lowering product quality to meet price targets
options.c: Restricting product availability to create scarcity
options.d: Building relationships with internal and external stakeholders

questions.explanation: Good communication lets a business keep employees, customers, suppliers and other stakeholders informed and engaged, which builds trust and long-term relationships. Option A works against this goal, while Options B and C are product and distribution choices that have nothing to do with the communication process.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Which of the following is a common form of business communication?

options.a: Product manufacturing and quality control
options.b: Financial forecasting and risk assessment
options.c: Machine maintenance scheduling
options.d: Presentations used to align a team on its objectives

questions.explanation: A presentation is a form of business communication that combines spoken words with visual aids to share information and get a group working toward the same goals. Options A, B and C are operational or financial tasks rather than ways of exchanging messages.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The communication model is significant because it helps to:

options.a: Identify barriers that can stop a message from being delivered and understood
options.b: Suppress feedback so the sender stays in control
options.c: Cut advertising spending without any plan
options.d: Reduce the number of products a firm sells

questions.explanation: By breaking communication into parts (sender, message, channel, receiver, feedback and noise), the model helps a business spot where a message can go wrong, for example a poor channel or a confusing message. Option B is wrong because feedback is a part of the model that should be encouraged, and Options C and D are budget and product decisions.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The process of transmitting information and shared meaning from one person or group to another person or group is called:

options.a: Perception
options.b: Negotiation
options.c: Communication
options.d: Motivation

questions.explanation: Communication is the transfer of information and shared meaning between a sender and a receiver. Option A is how a person interprets what they sense, and option B is bargaining to reach an agreement; both may involve communication but neither is the general process of passing meaning.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The word 'communication' comes from the Latin word 'communis'. What does 'communis' mean?

options.a: Common
options.b: Message
options.c: Speech
options.d: Exchange of goods

questions.explanation: 'Communis' means common, which reflects the idea that communication aims to create a common or shared understanding between sender and receiver. Option B and option C are things used in communicating, not the meaning of the Latin root.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Business communication is best described as:

options.a: The use of paid mass media by a firm to promote its products to the general public
options.b: The exchange of information between people within and outside an organisation in order to achieve the organisation's goals
options.c: The face-to-face presentation of a product by a salesperson to a prospective buyer
options.d: The private conversations of employees about matters unrelated to their work

questions.explanation: Business communication covers all the information sharing that takes place inside a firm and between the firm and outsiders such as customers, suppliers and regulators, for the purpose of running the business. Option A is advertising and option C is personal selling, which are only specific promotional uses of communication.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of business communication?

options.a: To remove the need for planning and organising in the firm
options.b: To persuade customers and other stakeholders to take action
options.c: To coordinate the work of different departments
options.d: To inform employees and customers about decisions and offers

questions.explanation: Communication supports planning and organising; it cannot replace them, so option A is not a purpose. Informing (option D), persuading (option B) and coordinating (option C) are all standard purposes of business communication.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: In the communication process, the act of putting thoughts or ideas into symbolic form, such as words, pictures or sounds, is known as:

options.a: Feedback
options.b: Decoding
options.c: Noise
options.d: Encoding

questions.explanation: Encoding is done by the sender, who converts an idea into symbols the receiver can understand. Option B is the reverse step, where the receiver interprets those symbols, and option A is the receiver's response sent back to the sender.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The process by which the receiver assigns meaning to the symbols sent by the sender is called:

options.a: Transmission
options.b: Encoding
options.c: Decoding
options.d: Feedback

questions.explanation: Decoding happens at the receiver's end, when the words, pictures or sounds received are interpreted and given meaning. Option B is done by the sender before the message is sent, and option A is simply the movement of the message through a channel.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: In the communication model, 'noise' refers to:

options.a: Any unplanned interference or distortion that prevents the message from being received as intended
options.b: The loud music used in radio and television advertisements
options.c: The medium through which the message travels from sender to receiver
options.d: The receiver's reply to the sender after receiving the message

questions.explanation: Noise is anything that disrupts or distorts communication, whether physical (such as a loud generator) or psychological (such as distraction). Option B takes the word too literally, option D describes feedback, and option C describes the channel.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Feedback in the communication process is best defined as:

options.a: The first message the sender transmits to the receiver
options.b: The distortion that occurs while the message is in the channel
options.c: The symbols the sender chooses to express an idea
options.d: The part of the receiver's response that is communicated back to the sender

questions.explanation: Feedback is the receiver's reaction returned to the sender, which tells the sender whether the message was understood. It turns communication into a two-way process. Option C is encoding and option B is noise.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The means or path through which a message travels from the sender to the receiver, such as radio, email or a face-to-face meeting, is called the:

options.a: Encoder
options.b: Field of experience
options.c: Decoder
options.d: Channel

questions.explanation: The channel (or medium) is the vehicle that carries the message, for example a phone call, a newspaper or social media. Option A and option C are the people who create and interpret the message, while option B is the background knowledge each party brings.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: In the communication process, the sender (source) is:

options.a: The reaction of the audience after seeing the message
options.b: The medium used to carry the message
options.c: The person or organisation that has an idea to share and starts the communication
options.d: The person or group for whom the message is intended

questions.explanation: The sender is where communication begins: the party with information to share who then encodes it into a message. Option D describes the receiver, option B the channel and option A the response.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The marketing manager of a Lagos cement company wants customers to see the brand as strong and durable. She works with an agency to turn this idea into a TV script showing a building standing firm in heavy rain. In the communication process, this activity is:

options.a: Noise
options.b: Encoding
options.c: Decoding
options.d: Feedback

questions.explanation: Converting the idea 'strong and durable' into pictures, words and sound is encoding, done on the sender's side. Option C would be the viewers interpreting the advert, and option D would be their response coming back to the company.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: A viewer in Ibadan watches a soft drink advert showing friends laughing at a party and concludes that the drink is for happy social occasions. Which stage of the communication process does this illustrate?

options.a: Channel selection
options.b: Encoding
options.c: Decoding
options.d: Feedback

questions.explanation: The viewer is interpreting the symbols in the advert and giving them meaning, which is decoding. Option B is what the advertiser did when creating the advert, and option D would only occur if the viewer sent a response back, for example by commenting or buying.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: A trader at Balogun Market cannot hear the details of a bank's radio jingle because of a loud generator nearby. In the communication model, the generator sound is an example of:

options.a: Feedback
options.b: Encoding
options.c: Decoding
options.d: Noise

questions.explanation: Noise is any interference that stops a message from being received as intended, and a loud generator is a classic physical noise. Option A would be the trader's response to the bank, while options B and C are the sending and interpreting stages, not interference.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: A telecoms company sends an SMS offering a N1,000 data bundle. Many customers reply 'YES' to subscribe, and others call the helpline to ask questions. These replies and calls represent:

options.a: Feedback
options.b: The channel
options.c: Noise
options.d: Encoding

questions.explanation: Feedback is the receiver's response sent back to the sender; the replies and calls tell the company how the message was received. Option B would be the SMS itself as the medium, and option C would be something that disrupted the message.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: An insurance agent explains a policy to market women in Aba using terms like 'indemnity', 'actuarial loading' and 'subrogation'. The women leave confused. This is mainly an example of which barrier to communication?

options.a: Information overload
options.b: Semantic (language) barrier
options.c: Organisational barrier
options.d: Physical barrier

questions.explanation: A semantic barrier arises when words, technical terms or jargon are not understood in the same way by sender and receiver. Nothing physical blocked the message (option D), and the problem is not too many messages (option A) but unfamiliar language.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: A customer whose account was wrongly debited is so angry that he does not listen to the bank officer's explanation. Which barrier to communication is mainly at work?

options.a: Physical barrier
options.b: Psychological (emotional) barrier
options.c: Semantic barrier
options.d: Cultural barrier

questions.explanation: Strong emotions such as anger, fear or distrust stop people from receiving messages properly, which is a psychological barrier. The officer's language is not the problem (option C), and there is no distance or physical interference (option A).

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: A foreign company runs an advert in Nigeria using a hand gesture that is friendly in its home country but considered rude by many Nigerians. This problem is best described as a:

options.a: Physical barrier
options.b: Semantic barrier caused by jargon
options.c: Cultural barrier
options.d: Organisational barrier

questions.explanation: Cultural barriers arise when symbols, gestures or customs mean different things in different cultures, so the receiver decodes the message differently from what the sender intended. Option A involves distance or interference, and option D relates to structures inside an organisation.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an element of the basic communication process model?

options.a: Noise
options.b: Budget
options.c: Feedback
options.d: Encoding

questions.explanation: The basic model is made up of the sender, encoding, message, channel, decoding, receiver, response, feedback and noise. A budget matters when planning a campaign, but it is not part of the communication process itself, whereas options D, A and C are all elements of the model.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: A bank officer receives over 200 emails a day, and important messages from her manager are often missed or read late. This barrier to communication is called:

options.a: Information overload
options.b: Semantic barrier
options.c: Selective retention
options.d: Cultural barrier

questions.explanation: Information overload happens when a receiver gets more messages than he or she can process, so some are ignored or misunderstood. Option B is about words being misunderstood, and option C is about remembering only messages that agree with one's beliefs.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The tendency of people to notice and interpret messages in a way that fits their existing beliefs and attitudes, while ignoring others, is called:

options.a: Selective perception
options.b: Information overload
options.c: Encoding
options.d: Feedback

questions.explanation: Selective perception means receivers filter messages through their own beliefs, so the same message may be understood differently by different people. Option B is about having too many messages, not filtering them by belief, and option C is done by the sender.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: According to the field of experience idea in communication, communication is most effective when:

options.a: The sender uses as many technical terms as possible
options.b: The sender's and receiver's backgrounds, knowledge and experiences overlap
options.c: The receiver has no previous knowledge of the subject
options.d: The message is sent without expecting any response

questions.explanation: The more the sender's and receiver's fields of experience overlap, the more likely the receiver is to decode the message as the sender intended. Option A usually reduces understanding, and option D removes feedback, which weakens communication.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The main weakness of the linear (one-way) model of communication is that it:

options.a: Does not include a sender
options.b: Does not include feedback from the receiver
options.c: Does not include a channel
options.d: Does not include a message

questions.explanation: The linear model shows communication flowing in one direction only, from sender to receiver, so it ignores the receiver's response. A sender, message and channel (options A, D and C) are all present in the linear model.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Which communication model, developed in 1949 from work on telephone signals, is best known for introducing the idea of 'noise' into communication?

options.a: AIDA model
options.b: Lasswell's model
options.c: Shannon and Weaver model
options.d: Schramm's model

questions.explanation: The Shannon and Weaver model, a linear model based on telephone transmission, introduced noise as anything that distorts the signal between sender and receiver. Option B is the 'who says what' verbal model, and option A describes the stages a buyer goes through (attention, interest, desire, action).

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: 'Who says what, in which channel, to whom, with what effect?' is a famous description of communication associated with:

options.a: Philip Kotler
options.b: Wilbur Schramm
options.c: Shannon and Weaver
options.d: Harold Lasswell

questions.explanation: Lasswell summarised communication as who (sender) says what (message) in which channel to whom (receiver) with what effect. Option C is linked with the noise idea, option B with the field of experience idea, and option A is a marketing writer rather than the author of this formula.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: In the transactional model of communication, communication is seen as:

options.a: A process in which noise never occurs
options.b: A continuous process in which both parties send and receive messages at the same time
options.c: A one-way flow from sender to a passive receiver
options.d: A process that has no channel

questions.explanation: The transactional model treats both parties as communicators who send and receive messages at the same time, for example through words and facial reactions during a conversation. Option C describes the linear model, and noise can occur in any model (option A).

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of non-verbal communication?

options.a: A sales letter
options.b: A salesperson's smile and firm handshake
options.c: A product brochure text
options.d: A telephone conversation

questions.explanation: Non-verbal communication sends messages without words, through facial expressions, gestures, posture, touch and appearance. Options A, D and C all rely on words, whether written or spoken.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The aspects of the voice, such as tone, pitch, speed and volume, that add meaning to spoken words are known as:

options.a: Proxemics
options.b: Kinesics
options.c: Haptics
options.d: Paralanguage

questions.explanation: Paralanguage is how something is said rather than the words themselves; a shouted 'thank you' means something different from a warm one. Option A is the use of space, option B is body movement and option C is touch.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The study of how people use personal space and distance when communicating is called:

options.a: Proxemics
options.b: Kinesics
options.c: Chronemics
options.d: Paralanguage

questions.explanation: Proxemics deals with space, for example how close a salesperson stands to a customer. Option B is body movement, option D is voice qualities and option C is the use of time.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Communication through body movements such as gestures, posture, facial expressions and eye contact is known as:

options.a: Paralanguage
options.b: Proxemics
options.c: Chronemics
options.d: Kinesics

questions.explanation: Kinesics, often called body language, covers gestures, posture, facial expression and eye contact. Option B is about space and option C is about time, such as punctuality.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: A supplier keeps a client waiting for two hours past their scheduled meeting in Abuja. The client concludes the supplier does not value the business. This message was sent through:

options.a: Chronemics (the use of time)
options.b: Haptics (touch)
options.c: Paralanguage
options.d: Written communication

questions.explanation: Chronemics is non-verbal communication through time, such as punctuality and waiting, and lateness often signals disrespect. No voice tone (option C), touch (option B) or written words (option D) carried this message.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a form of non-verbal communication?

options.a: A memo sent to all staff
options.b: Eye contact
options.c: Tone of voice
options.d: Dress and appearance

questions.explanation: A memo uses written words, so it is verbal (written) communication. Eye contact (option B), tone of voice (option C) and dress (option D) all communicate without the actual words being the message.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The main advantage of oral communication over written communication is that it:

options.a: Is always more suitable for legal agreements
options.b: Provides a permanent record for future reference
options.c: Can be checked and edited carefully before it is received
options.d: Allows immediate feedback and clarification

questions.explanation: In oral communication, such as a meeting or phone call, the receiver can respond and ask questions at once, so misunderstandings are cleared quickly. Options B, A and C are advantages of written communication, not oral.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Which of the following is a major advantage of written communication?

options.a: It provides a permanent record that can serve as evidence
options.b: It allows tone of voice to show the sender's feelings
options.c: It is always faster than speaking face to face
options.d: It gives instant feedback through facial expressions

questions.explanation: Written messages such as letters, contracts and emails can be stored and referred to later, which makes them useful as records and evidence. Options D and B are features of oral communication, and written communication is usually slower, not faster (option C).

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: A distributor in Kano agrees with a manufacturer on credit terms of N5 million payable in 60 days. Both want terms that can be relied on if there is a dispute later. The best form of communication for this is:

options.a: Written communication, such as a signed agreement
options.b: Non-verbal communication
options.c: Oral communication in a phone call
options.d: Informal grapevine communication

questions.explanation: Written communication creates a permanent, signed record that can be used as evidence in a dispute. A phone call (option C) leaves no reliable record, and the grapevine (option D) is unofficial and unreliable.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Formal communication in an organisation refers to communication that:

options.a: Is always oral rather than written
options.b: Takes place only outside working hours
options.c: Spreads through friendships and casual conversations among staff
options.d: Follows official channels and lines of authority set by the organisation

questions.explanation: Formal communication flows through the official structure, such as reports, memos and meetings between managers and their staff. Option C describes informal communication (the grapevine), and formal messages can be written or oral, so option A is wrong.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The informal network through which news and rumours spread among employees, outside official channels, is called the:

options.a: Formal network
options.b: Downward channel
options.c: Grapevine
options.d: Chain of command

questions.explanation: The grapevine is the unofficial, informal communication network in an organisation. Option D is the official line of authority, and option B is formal communication from superiors to subordinates.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The Managing Director of a Lagos manufacturing firm sends a circular to all staff explaining a new resumption time. This is an example of:

options.a: Downward communication
options.b: Upward communication
options.c: Grapevine communication
options.d: Horizontal communication

questions.explanation: Downward communication flows from higher levels of authority to lower levels, for example instructions, policies and circulars. Option B flows from subordinates to superiors, and option C flows between people at the same level.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Sales representatives of a beverage company in Port Harcourt submit weekly sales reports to their regional manager. This is an example of:

options.a: External communication
options.b: Horizontal communication
options.c: Upward communication
options.d: Downward communication

questions.explanation: Upward communication flows from subordinates to superiors, for example reports, suggestions and complaints. Option D would be the manager instructing the reps, and option A would involve people outside the company.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The marketing manager and the production manager of a company, who are at the same level, meet to agree on when a new product will be ready for launch. This is:

options.a: Horizontal (lateral) communication
options.b: Downward communication
options.c: External communication
options.d: Upward communication

questions.explanation: Horizontal communication takes place between people or departments at the same level and is mainly used for coordination. Neither manager is above the other, so options B and D do not apply, and both are inside the firm (option C).

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of upward communication?

options.a: A supervisor's instructions to the team
options.b: A job description given to a new employee
options.c: An employee suggestion box
options.d: A memo announcing a new company policy

questions.explanation: A suggestion box carries ideas and complaints from employees up to management, so it is upward communication. Options B, D and A all move from management down to employees.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: A bank issues a press release to newspapers announcing that its mobile app has been upgraded. This is mainly an example of:

options.a: Upward communication
options.b: Horizontal communication
options.c: External communication
options.d: Internal communication

questions.explanation: External communication is between the organisation and outsiders such as customers, the media, suppliers and regulators. Option D would be messages among the bank's own staff, and options A and B describe directions of flow inside an organisation.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of internal communication?

options.a: A letter of complaint to a supplier
options.b: A billboard advertisement
options.c: A product launch press conference
options.d: A staff newsletter

questions.explanation: Internal communication takes place among members of the organisation, and a staff newsletter is written for employees. Options B, A and C are all aimed at people outside the firm.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The main disadvantage of the grapevine as a channel of communication is that:

options.a: It cannot exist in large organisations
options.b: Messages are often distorted and can spread false rumours
options.c: It can only carry written messages
options.d: It is always slower than formal channels

questions.explanation: Because the grapevine is unofficial and passes from person to person, messages are often incomplete or distorted, and rumours can spread. In fact the grapevine is usually very fast (so option D is wrong), and it exists in organisations of every size (option A).

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Which of the following is generally considered an advantage of the grapevine?

options.a: It is controlled by top management
options.b: Its messages are always accurate
options.c: It provides official records of decisions
options.d: It spreads information very quickly

questions.explanation: The grapevine is known for its speed, since news passes quickly through informal networks of friends and colleagues. It is not always accurate (option B), management cannot control it (option A), and it does not create official records (option C).

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a barrier to effective communication?

options.a: Physical noise
options.b: Use of jargon
options.c: Active listening
options.d: Emotional stress

questions.explanation: Active listening means paying full attention, asking questions and confirming understanding, so it improves communication rather than blocking it. Jargon (option B), physical noise (option A) and emotional stress (option D) are all common barriers.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Which of the following is the best way to overcome barriers to communication?

options.a: Using simple language and encouraging feedback to check understanding
options.b: Using more technical terms to sound professional
options.c: Sending the same message through as many channels as possible at once
options.d: Avoiding questions from the receiver to save time

questions.explanation: Simple language reduces semantic barriers, and feedback lets the sender confirm that the message was understood as intended. Option B creates jargon problems, option C can cause information overload, and option D removes feedback.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: In the communication process, how does 'response' differ from 'feedback'?

options.a: Response is created by the sender, while feedback is created by the channel
options.b: Response happens before encoding, while feedback happens before decoding
options.c: Response is the receiver's reaction to the message, while feedback is the part of that reaction communicated back to the sender
options.d: Response and feedback are two words for noise in the channel

questions.explanation: After decoding, the receiver reacts in some way, which is the response, and the part of that reaction that reaches the sender is feedback. For example, a viewer may like an advert (response) and then post a comment to the brand (feedback). Options A, B and D misplace both terms in the process.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: In the communication process, the 'message' is:

options.a: The reply the receiver sends back to the sender
options.b: The interference that distorts communication
options.c: The set of words, pictures, sounds or symbols that the sender transmits
options.d: The person who receives and interprets the communication

questions.explanation: The message is the actual content the sender transmits after encoding, such as the words and pictures in an advert. Option D is the receiver, option B is noise and option A is feedback.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The receiver in the communication process is:

options.a: The person who creates and encodes the message
options.b: The person or group the message is intended for, who decodes it
options.c: The symbols used to express the message
options.d: The medium that carries the message

questions.explanation: The receiver is the target of the message and is responsible for decoding it into meaning. Option A is the sender, option D is the channel and option C is the message.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Communication is said to be effective when:

options.a: The receiver receives the message without any opportunity to respond
options.b: The message has been sent through the most expensive channel
options.c: The meaning understood by the receiver matches the meaning intended by the sender
options.d: The sender has transmitted the message, whether or not it is understood

questions.explanation: Effective communication is about shared meaning: the receiver understands what the sender meant. Merely sending a message (option D) does not guarantee understanding, and the cost of the channel (option B) is not the test.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Which of the following is the best example of one-way communication?

options.a: A telephone call with a customer
options.b: A roadside billboard advert
options.c: A face-to-face sales negotiation
options.d: A question-and-answer session at a meeting

questions.explanation: In one-way communication the message flows from sender to receiver with no direct chance for the receiver to respond, as with a billboard. Options C, A and D all allow immediate replies, so they are two-way.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: A channel's 'richness' is its ability to carry several cues and give immediate feedback. Which of the following is the richest communication channel?

options.a: An email
options.b: A face-to-face meeting
options.c: A printed notice
options.d: A formal report

questions.explanation: Face-to-face communication carries words, tone of voice, facial expressions and gestures, and allows instant feedback, so it is the richest channel. Printed notices, emails and reports (options C, A and D) carry mainly words and give slow or no feedback.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: The tendency of people to remember mainly the information that supports their existing beliefs and to forget information that does not is called:

options.a: Selective exposure
options.b: Selective retention
options.c: Encoding
options.d: Information overload

questions.explanation: Selective retention is about memory: people keep messages that agree with their beliefs and forget the rest. Option A is about which messages people choose to be exposed to in the first place, and option D is having too many messages to process.

questions.topic: Communication, Business Communication and the Communication Process
questions.question: Junior staff of a large Lagos firm are afraid to report problems directly to the Managing Director because of the many levels of authority and the MD's high status. This is mainly a:

options.a: Cultural barrier between countries
options.b: Physical noise
options.c: Semantic barrier
options.d: Organisational (status) barrier

questions.explanation: Organisational barriers come from the structure of the firm, such as too many levels in the hierarchy and status differences that discourage upward communication. The problem is not words (option C), national culture (option A) or physical interference (option B).

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: Marketing communication in the internet era is distinguished by:

options.a: Reliance only on traditional print and broadcast media
options.b: Use of social media platforms for two-way engagement with audiences
options.c: Exclusive use of personal selling
options.d: A sole focus on public relations campaigns

questions.explanation: The internet, and especially social media, turned marketing communication into a two-way conversation in which brands talk directly with customers and customers talk back. Option A describes the pre-internet era, and Options C and D are wrong because the word 'only' or 'exclusive' ignores the mix of tools firms use online.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: Online chat rooms and blogging websites, where many people exchange messages with many others, are examples of which type of communication?

options.a: One-to-many
options.b: Many-to-many
options.c: One-to-one
options.d: Many-to-one

questions.explanation: Many-to-many communication lets large numbers of people send and receive messages among themselves, and it has grown with the internet through chat rooms, blogs and social media. Option A is one sender broadcasting to many people, as in a TV advert, Option C is a personal exchange such as a sales presentation, and Option D is many people replying to one sender, such as replies to an email.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: Social media marketing is best described as:

options.a: Placing advertisements only in newspapers and magazines
options.b: Using platforms such as X (Twitter) and LinkedIn to deliver targeted, interactive content
options.c: Selling products door to door
options.d: Sending printed catalogues to customers by post

questions.explanation: Social media marketing means using social networks to share targeted content, interact with followers and promote a brand. Option A is print advertising, Option C is personal selling, and Option D is offline direct mail, none of which uses social platforms.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: The strategic role of social media in marketing communication is to:

options.a: Broadcast one-way messages while ignoring customer comments
options.b: Replace the need for any product quality
options.c: Foster dialogue, build communities and strengthen customer relationships
options.d: Cut advertising budgets without evaluation

questions.explanation: Social media is valuable because it lets brands hold conversations with customers, gather communities of fans and keep relationships going over time. Option A misses the point, since the strength of social media is its two-way nature, and Options B and D are not roles of communication at all.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: In the internet era, word-of-mouth communication has been:

options.a: Made less relevant than traditional advertising channels
options.b: Abandoned by businesses that want to keep control of messages
options.c: Amplified through online reviews, shares and influencer endorsements
options.d: Weakened because online noise stops people from hearing it

questions.explanation: Word-of-mouth is now amplified because a single customer review, post or share can reach thousands of people in minutes. Option A and Option D wrongly suggest it has lost influence, and Option B is wrong because firms actively encourage positive online word-of-mouth rather than abandon it.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: Social media marketing enables businesses to:

options.a: Reach only people who already buy the product
options.b: Avoid collecting any information about customers
options.c: Send the same message to everyone with no targeting
options.d: Deliver closely targeted messages based on data about their audience

questions.explanation: Social platforms collect data on users' interests, location and behaviour, so businesses can aim messages at the exact groups most likely to respond. Option C and Option B ignore this targeting ability, which also reaches new prospects, and Option A is the opposite of how these platforms work.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: Marketing communication in the internet era is characterised by:

options.a: Less customer interaction so that campaigns are simpler
options.b: Greater interactivity, real-time engagement and integration across many channels
options.c: Fewer advertising options because of digital saturation
options.d: Less feedback because online platforms limit responses

questions.explanation: The internet lets customers respond instantly, lets firms reply in real time, and allows the same campaign to run across websites, email, search and social media. Options A, C and D all suggest a reduction, when the internet has actually increased interaction, advertising options and feedback.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: A major function of social media in marketing communication is to:

options.a: Increase brand visibility, affinity and long-term loyalty
options.b: Avoid engaging with customers to save resources
options.c: Compromise product quality for profit
options.d: Restrict product availability to create exclusivity

questions.explanation: Regular, engaging social media activity keeps a brand in front of its audience, makes people like it more and encourages them to stay loyal. Option B defeats the purpose of social media, and Options C and D are product and distribution decisions rather than communication functions.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: Word-of-mouth communication remains important in the internet era because it:

options.a: Is fully controlled by the company that pays for it
options.b: Costs nothing and therefore needs no strategy
options.c: Builds trust, credibility and purchase intent through the influence of peers
options.d: Only spreads through face-to-face conversation

questions.explanation: People tend to trust recommendations from friends, family and other customers more than company adverts, so word-of-mouth strongly shapes buying decisions. Option A is wrong because word-of-mouth comes from customers and is not controlled by the firm, Option B ignores that firms still plan how to encourage it, and Option D ignores online reviews and shares.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: The effectiveness of social media marketing comes mainly from its ability to:

options.a: Send messages one way without customer responses
options.b: Enable two-way communication and real-time interaction with customers
options.c: Replace all other forms of marketing communication
options.d: Work without any content being created

questions.explanation: Social media lets customers comment, ask questions and share, and lets the brand reply immediately, which makes communication two-way and personal. Option A describes traditional one-way media, Option C overstates its role since firms still combine it with other tools, and Option D is wrong because social media depends on content.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: The internet has transformed marketing communication by:

options.a: Speeding up the spread of messages and widening their reach to global audiences
options.b: Reducing customer interaction to streamline efforts
options.c: Limiting advertising options to traditional media
options.d: Reducing feedback because of digital overload

questions.explanation: Online, a message can be published once and reach people across the world almost instantly, far faster and wider than traditional media. Options B, C and D describe the reverse of what happened, since the internet increased interaction, added new advertising options and made feedback easier.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: The role of social media in marketing communication includes:

options.a: Allowing direct engagement with customers and providing useful customer insights
options.b: Avoiding customer interaction to reduce costs
options.c: Removing the need for market research of any kind
options.d: Limiting a brand to a single target audience

questions.explanation: On social media, brands talk directly with customers, and the comments, likes and shares give them insight into what customers think and want. Option B is the opposite of engagement, Option C overstates things because social insight supports research rather than replacing it, and Option D is not a feature of social media.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: Online word-of-mouth is described as dynamic mainly because:

options.a: It is controlled entirely by the business
options.b: It is confined to traditional offline channels
options.c: Its impact can be positive or negative depending on customers' feelings and experiences
options.d: It always has the same effect on every brand

questions.explanation: Word-of-mouth reflects what customers actually experienced, so happy customers spread praise while unhappy ones spread complaints, and both can travel fast online. Option A is wrong because customers, not the business, create word-of-mouth, Option B ignores reviews and social posts, and Option D contradicts its changing nature.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: The most important change the internet and social media brought to marketing communication is that it shifted from:

options.a: A one-way monologue from firms to a two-way conversation between firms and customers
options.b: Targeted messages to messages for the whole population only
options.c: Customer-focused messages to product-focused messages
options.d: Paid communication to completely free communication for all firms

questions.explanation: Traditional mass media mainly let firms talk at customers, while the internet and social media let customers reply, comment and talk to each other, turning marketing into a two-way conversation. Online communication still has costs (option D), and it made targeting easier, not harder (option B).

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: In 1996, Hotmail added the line 'Get your free email at Hotmail' to every email its users sent and gained millions of users within months. This is a well-known early example of:

options.a: Sales promotion
options.b: Viral marketing
options.c: Personal selling
options.d: Outdoor advertising

questions.explanation: Viral marketing gets customers themselves to pass a message along, so it spreads rapidly from person to person; every Hotmail user who sent an email advertised the service. No salesperson was involved (option C), and no short-term incentive such as a discount was offered (option A).

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: Which platforms rose in the 2000s and changed how businesses interacted with their audiences by making marketing a two-way conversation?

options.a: MySpace, Facebook and Twitter
options.b: Newspapers and magazines
options.c: Radio and television
options.d: Billboards and posters

questions.explanation: Social media platforms such as MySpace, Facebook and Twitter appeared in the 2000s and allowed brands to engage directly with customers. Radio and television (option C) became important in the 20th century, and print media (option B) are much older.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: Online chat rooms, discussion forums and blogs, where many people communicate with many others at the same time, are examples of which type of communication made possible by the internet?

options.a: One-to-one
options.b: Many-to-many
options.c: Many-to-one
options.d: One-to-many

questions.explanation: Many-to-many communication lets large numbers of people exchange messages with each other, and it has grown with the internet through chat rooms, forums and blogs. Option D is a single broadcast to many, such as a TV news bulletin, and option A is a personal exchange, such as a sales negotiation.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: In the internet era, consumers can easily compare prices, read reviews and publicly share their opinions about brands. This has resulted in:

options.a: Firms gaining total control over what consumers hear about brands
options.b: Consumers depending only on advertising for product information
options.c: The end of the need for marketing communication
options.d: Greater consumer power and control over marketing communication

questions.explanation: The internet gives consumers access to information and a public voice, which shifts power towards them. Firms now have less control over what is said about them (option A), and consumers rely on many sources besides advertising (option B).

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: Social media marketing is best defined as:

options.a: Using social media platforms to engage audiences, build the brand, and drive traffic and sales
options.b: Sending printed catalogues to customers' homes
options.c: Placing adverts only on television and radio
options.d: Selling products only through face-to-face meetings in social gatherings

questions.explanation: Social media marketing uses platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, X, TikTok and LinkedIn to share content, interact with customers and promote the brand. Option D is personal selling, option C is traditional broadcast advertising, and option B is offline direct mail.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: User-generated content (UGC) refers to:

options.a: Content such as reviews, photos and videos about a brand that is created by customers rather than by the brand
options.b: Adverts written by a firm's advertising agency
options.c: Press releases issued by a firm's public relations department
options.d: Product information printed on the package by the manufacturer

questions.explanation: UGC is created by consumers themselves, for example product reviews, unboxing videos and posts using a brand's hashtag. Options B, C and D are all created or controlled by the firm or its agents.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: Customers of a Lekki restaurant post their own photos and short videos of its jollof rice on Instagram and TikTok with the restaurant's hashtag, without being paid. These posts are best described as:

options.a: Paid media advertising
options.b: User-generated content
options.c: Sales promotion
options.d: Personal selling

questions.explanation: Content created and shared voluntarily by customers about a brand is user-generated content. It is not paid media (option A) because the restaurant did not pay for the posts, and no salesperson or price incentive is involved (options D and C).

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: Viral marketing is best described as:

options.a: Reducing prices for a short period to attract buyers
options.b: Advertising medicines and health products
options.c: Creating content so interesting that people pass it on to others, spreading it rapidly online
options.d: Sending the same advert to customers several times a day

questions.explanation: Viral marketing is often called the internet version of word-of-mouth: the content is so engaging that consumers share it, so it spreads like a virus. Option B takes the word 'viral' literally, option D is simply repetition, and option A is sales promotion.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
questions.question: Word-of-mouth (WOM) communication refers to:

options.a: Formal sales presentations made by a firm's sales force
options.b: Paid announcements read by radio presenters
options.c: Informal person-to-person communication among consumers about products, services and brands
options.d: Messages printed on a product's label

questions.explanation: Word-of-mouth is when customers share their experiences and opinions about products with friends, family and peers. Paid announcements (option B) are advertising, and sales presentations (option A) are personal selling, both controlled by the firm.

questions.topic: MarCom in the Internet Era, Social Media and Word-of-Mouth
